btos.label: Real estate and rental and leasing (NAICS 53)

name: Real Estate
blurb: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest AI and now federally regulated under FHFA and CFPB quality-control rules; plus valuation, leasing, and property-management platforms with methodology disclosed.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports real-estate sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The interagency Quality Control Standards for Automated Valuation Models - finalized by FHFA, CFPB, and the banking regulators - are the first binding federal rules for the sector's core AI: the models that value homes in mortgage decisions.
points.name: AVMs are now federally regulated AI

points.desc: The bureau's AVM rule page and its algorithmic-appraisal work are the record of how valuation bias and model accountability are supervised.
points.name: CFPB carries the consumer-protection side

points.desc: The National Association of Realtors' technology research tracks what AI tools agents and brokerages actually adopt.
points.name: NAR surveys the profession

points.desc: The Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation publishes the funding data on AI and proptech startups - the sector's investment barometer.
points.name: CRETI tracks proptech capital

points.name: Zillow and Redfin publish their valuation models

points.desc: The iBuyer's pricing models carry real balance-sheet exposure - its own filings and documentation are the record of valuation AI with capital consequences.
points.name: Opendoor prices houses with models at risk

points.desc: JLL and CBRE - the commercial real estate services majors - deploy generative and predictive AI across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics.
points.name: The CRE giants run enterprise AI

points.name: Leasing and property ops are automating

points.name: CREtech and MetaProp track the proptech market

points.desc: The Building Owners and Managers Association tracks AI in smart-building operations, energy efficiency, and predictive maintenance across commercial property.
points.name: BOMA covers commercial building operations

points.desc: The realtor association's technology accelerator is where residential proptech gets vetted and scaled - a window into which tools the profession is actually adopting.
points.name: NAR REACH backs the startups

points.desc: The residential brokerage's platform applies AI to agent workflows, client matching, and predictive listing recommendations.
points.name: Compass runs AI inside the brokerage workflow

points.desc: HouseCanary's valuation and forecasting models and Cherre's data integration layer are what institutional investors underwrite on - the wholesale side of the AVM story.
points.name: Institutional valuation runs on data platforms

points.desc: Prophia extracts terms, rent rolls, and obligations from commercial leases automatically - one of the clearest production uses of document AI in the sector.
points.name: Lease abstraction is a document-AI problem

points.desc: Visitt and Building Engines apply IoT sensing and machine learning to HVAC optimization, maintenance prediction, and tenant workflow in operating buildings.
points.name: Smart buildings close the operations loop

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.0% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the latest reference period, up from 25.6% in the prior period, making it one of the more measurably active sectors in the survey. The increase is gradual but consistent, and because the Census question asks about actual use in the prior two weeks rather than intentions or pilots, the figure reflects deployed technology rather than aspiration.

The longest-established AI application in the sector is automated valuation. Zillow publishes Zestimates for more than 110 million homes using a neural network model that draws on county and tax assessor records, MLS feeds, listing signals, and user-submitted data, with Zillow noting that improvements to the architecture have helped reduce overall error rates while maintaining broad coverage. HouseCanary provides AI-powered valuations, forecasts, and analytics covering over 136 million U.S. properties, combining machine learning with image recognition that identifies room types and assesses home condition from photos. Opendoor has carried this further by using pricing models to make direct purchase offers to homeowners, a structure that places real balance-sheet exposure behind the model's output. These consumer and institutional valuation tools now operate under binding federal oversight: the FHFA, CFPB, OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, and NCUA jointly finalized quality control standards for automated valuation models used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers, requiring institutions to maintain policies that ensure a high level of confidence in estimates, protect against data manipulation, avoid conflicts of interest, and conduct random sample testing and reviews.

On the commercial side, AI is concentrating in leasing communications, document processing, and building operations. EliseAI offers an agentic conversational platform that handles inbound messages and calls around the clock, schedules tours, follows up with prospects, and manages maintenance requests automatically, with the company positioning the tool as freeing staff for higher-value work. Prophia applies AI to lease abstraction, extracting key terms and combining that output with expert validation to produce structured lease data for portfolio management and risk identification. Building Engines, described as a JLL company, offers a property management platform whose Prism AI layer delivers instant answers, recommendations, and automation aimed at cutting costs and growing net operating income. Matterport digitizes physical space through 3D cameras and virtual tour software, integrating with construction platforms such as Procore and Autodesk and incorporating real-time AWS data to support portfolio management and reduce site visits.

Among the larger enterprise players, JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, applying it across brokerage, facilities management, and portfolio analytics. Compass integrates AI into agent workflows within its residential brokerage platform. The proptech ecosystem supporting these deployments is organized in part through CREtech, whose annual New York conference draws executives from across the ownership, investment, brokerage, and technology spectrum, and through CRETI, the Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation, which tracks the health of the proptech sector. NAR REACH, the technology scale-up program created by Second Century Ventures, serves as an accelerator for residential proptech startups and provides a window into which tools the profession is moving toward adoption.

The regulatory posture is more developed here than in most sectors precisely because valuation AI touches mortgage collateral and therefore consumer financial protection. The interagency AVM rule is the clearest example in any industry of federal regulators naming a specific category of machine learning model and imposing governance requirements on it. For firms deploying AVMs in credit decisions or securitization, compliance with those quality control standards is now mandatory rather than best practice. Fair lending risk, meaning the possibility that model outputs systematically disadvantage protected classes, is the dimension the CFPB's involvement most directly signals, and any institution using algorithmic appraisal tools in lending workflows should treat that as an active supervisory concern rather than a theoretical one.

For a decision-maker evaluating AI deployment in real estate, the sector's experience suggests that the clearest near-term value sits in document-heavy workflows such as lease abstraction, in resident and prospect communications where round-the-clock response has measurable operational consequences, and in valuation support where commercial data platforms can reduce underwriting time. The regulatory environment rewards institutions that can demonstrate model governance, auditability, and bias testing, particularly on the valuation side, so those capabilities are not optional for firms in the mortgage or secondary market space. The gap between the 28.0% adoption figure and full deployment suggests meaningful room for expansion, but the firms moving fastest are those with structured data assets, clear workflows to automate, and the compliance infrastructure to satisfy the oversight that the FHFA and CFPB have now formalized.
